comment: One line per scene, spoken conversationally in the first person: what the thing is, what is live today, and what is still to build. Times are the scene windows in the 90s composition; each clip must fit its window with ~0.5s lead-in. Numbers are written out to steer TTS pronunciation.

lines.text: Alright, so this is RelayOps, and here's what I've actually got running so far.
The idea's simple. A broker's watching dozens of trucks, but only a few need a person right now. So the board's whole job is to surface those few, and to stay honest about the ones it can't see.

Take this late load. Every figure here is computed, not guessed. Its last known position plus the drive time left puts it thirty-eight minutes past the appointment. No language model touches that math, and the timestamp it's based on travels with the number.

And it shows its work. Before it alerts anyone it walks a checklist: pickup still open, appointment on file, tracking fresh, E T A computed, past the threshold, recipient verified, nothing sent already. Only when every box is ticked does it queue exactly one notification.

Now the honest part. This truck hasn't reported in forty-two minutes, so rather than invent an E T A, the agent returns nothing, reason: tracking stale, and stays quiet. And it counts that silence, because a non-action you can't see looks just like a bug.

The thing I cared most about is never double-sending. Two scanners can hit the same load at the same instant, but only one insert wins. The other gets a unique conflict and reads back the winner's row. One goal, one alert, zero duplicates, enforced by the database, not by a worker's memory.
So that's what's live, and you can try it online right now. Next up: notifications, the queue, and the inbound email agent.
